sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About EGFR Mutation Lung Cancer: Osimertinib and Beyond
sectionToMerge.intro: These questions explain EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer, how osimertinib and related targeted therapies work, and what patients and caregivers should discuss with their oncology team.

groups.title: Understanding EGFR Mutation Lung Cancer and Osimertinib

items.q: What is an EGFR mutation in lung cancer?
items.a: An EGFR mutation is a change in the epidermal growth factor receptor gene that can drive certain non-small cell lung cancers to grow. It is found most often in lung adenocarcinoma, in non-smokers, and in some Asian populations, though it can occur in anyone. Identifying an EGFR mutation through biomarker testing helps the oncology team decide whether targeted therapy, rather than standard chemotherapy alone, may be suitable for a particular patient.

items.q: What is osimertinib and how does it work?
items.a: Osimertinib is a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor taken as a daily oral tablet. It works by blocking abnormal signals from the mutated EGFR protein that tell cancer cells to grow and divide. It is designed to target common EGFR mutations and the T790M resistance mutation, and it can also reach cancer that has spread to the brain. Suitability and dosing should always be confirmed by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Which EGFR mutations respond to osimertinib?
items.a: Osimertinib mainly targets the common sensitizing EGFR mutations, exon 19 deletions and the exon 21 L858R mutation, and the T790M resistance mutation. Some less common mutations may respond variably, while others, such as certain exon 20 insertions, generally do not. Because response depends on the exact mutation, complete biomarker testing is essential. Final treatment choice should be based on the pathology report and reviewed by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: How is an EGFR mutation detected?
items.a: An EGFR mutation is detected through molecular testing of tumour tissue from a biopsy or, in some cases, a blood-based liquid biopsy. Techniques such as PCR or next-generation sequencing identify the specific mutation and help guide targeted treatment. Testing may take one to two weeks depending on the laboratory. Accurate results depend on adequate sample quality, so the treating team may recommend repeat or additional testing when needed.

items.q: Who is eligible for osimertinib treatment?
items.a: Osimertinib may be considered for patients with non-small cell lung cancer that carries a sensitizing EGFR mutation confirmed by biomarker testing. Eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, mutation profile, previous treatment, and overall health. It is used in advanced disease and, in selected cases, after surgery for earlier-stage EGFR-mutant lung cancer. Final decisions about starting osimertinib should be made by the treating oncology team after reviewing the complete medical picture.

items.q: Is osimertinib used as a first-line treatment?
items.a: Osimertinib is often used as a first-line treatment for advanced EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer in many countries. Starting with osimertinib early may be preferred because it targets both common EGFR mutations and can act on cancer that has spread to the brain. However, treatment sequencing depends on the mutation, disease stage, and individual factors, and the right approach should be decided by the treating oncology team.

items.q: What are the common side effects of osimertinib?
items.a: Common side effects of osimertinib include diarrhoea, skin rash, dry skin, nail changes, and mouth sores, which are often manageable. Less commonly, it may affect the heart rhythm, blood counts, or lungs, so regular monitoring is important. Patients should report new breathlessness, fever, or unusual symptoms promptly. Side effects vary between individuals, and any dose adjustments or supportive care should be guided by the treating medical team.

items.q: How is response to treatment monitored?
items.a: Response to osimertinib is monitored mainly through periodic imaging, such as CT scans, and clinical review of symptoms and overall condition. Doctors compare scans over time to see whether the cancer is shrinking, stable, or progressing. Blood tests and, in some cases, liquid biopsies may also be used. Monitoring schedules vary by patient, and any changes to treatment should be decided by the treating oncology team based on these results.

The cost of osimertinib varies widely by country, brand, dose, and whether generic versions are available. In some countries, generic or subsidised options can significantly reduce the monthly cost compared with the originator brand. Final expenses also depend on tests, doctor visits, imaging, and duration of treatment. Because pricing changes over time, patients should confirm current costs with their treating hospital or pharmacy rather than relying on fixed figures.

Osimertinib is available in India, including originator and generic versions, which can make targeted therapy more affordable for many patients. It is prescribed at major cancer centres for eligible patients with EGFR-mutant lung cancer confirmed by biomarker testing. Availability, brand choice, and pricing may vary between hospitals and pharmacies. A qualified oncology team should confirm suitability, dosing, and monitoring before starting or changing treatment.

EGFR-targeted therapies, including osimertinib and other tyrosine kinase inhibitors, are available in many countries with established cancer care, such as India, China, Singapore, Turkey, and others. Access to specific drugs, generics, and clinical trials can differ between countries and hospitals. Choosing where to seek treatment depends on the mutation, available options, cost, and travel considerations, and should be discussed with a qualified oncology team before making arrangements.

items.q: What happens when osimertinib stops working?
items.a: When osimertinib stops working, it usually means the cancer has developed resistance and started to progress. At this point, doctors often recommend repeat biomarker testing, sometimes with a new biopsy or liquid biopsy, to understand the resistance mechanism. The next step may involve chemotherapy, combination approaches, or a clinical trial. The most appropriate option depends on the individual situation and should be decided by the treating oncology team.

items.q: What treatments are available after osimertinib resistance?
items.a: After osimertinib resistance, options may include platinum-based chemotherapy, chemotherapy combined with other agents, and newer targeted or antibody-based treatments studied in trials. The choice depends on the resistance mechanism found on repeat testing, overall health, and prior treatments. Some patients may be candidates for clinical trials exploring emerging therapies. There is no single best option for everyone, so decisions should be guided by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for EGFR-mutant lung cancer?
items.a: Yes, there are clinical trials studying new drugs and combinations for EGFR-mutant lung cancer, including options for patients whose cancer has progressed on osimertinib. Trials may test next-generation inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates, or combination strategies. Eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Participation does not guarantee benefit, so it should be discussed carefully with the treating oncology team.

items.q: What is the role of combination therapy?
items.a: Combination therapy aims to improve outcomes by pairing an EGFR inhibitor with chemotherapy or other targeted agents, and it is an active area of research. Some combinations may help control disease longer in selected patients, but they can also increase side effects. Whether a combination is appropriate depends on the mutation, stage, overall health, and current evidence. These decisions should be made by a qualified oncology team after careful review.

items.q: What reports are needed for EGFR-targeted treatment abroad?
items.a: For EGFR-targeted treatment abroad, patients usually need recent pathology and biopsy reports, biomarker or molecular testing showing the EGFR mutation, imaging such as CT or PET scans, and a summary of previous treatments. Blood test results and a current clinical summary are also helpful. Complete, up-to-date records allow the specialist team to assess suitability accurately. The treating hospital may request additional tests before confirming a treatment plan.

items.q: How can international patients access osimertinib and beyond?
items.a: International patients can access osimertinib and further treatments by sharing their medical reports with an appropriate cancer centre for review, then planning travel if treatment is confirmed. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, travel fitness, and the patient's condition. A second opinion, cost estimate, and follow-up plan are often useful before travelling. Hospital admission and treatment acceptance cannot be guaranteed and depend on the specialist team's assessment.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with EGFR mutation lung cancer?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is intended to make the process clearer and more manageable, not to replace the guidance of the treating doctors and hospital.
